analysis.one_liner: Exempts replacement parts for existing products from federal restrictions on toxic chemicals.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 21, 2026 with one cosponsor, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the nation's main toxic-chemical law, the EPA can restrict chemicals found to pose unreasonable risk. This bill would require the EPA to exempt replacement parts for cars, appliances, electronics, and other complex products if those products were designed before a restriction rule was published. The EPA could only regulate such a part if it proved, with substantial evidence, that the part by itself significantly drives the health risk, and even then it would have to allow at least a 10-year transition. It would also bar the EPA from banning the manufacture or import of a chemical when that chemical is needed to make the exempted parts.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of replacement parts and of complex durable goods (automakers, appliance and electronics makers) gain a guaranteed exemption from chemical restrictions for parts serving pre-rule product designs, avoiding the cost of reformulating or retooling. Chemical suppliers keep a market for substances the EPA has restricted elsewhere. Owners of older products also benefit in a narrower way: parts containing restricted chemicals would stay on the market, so a restriction rule could not strand them without repair options.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parts makers, automakers, appliance and electronics firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the EPA to exempt replacement parts for complex durable goods and complex consumer goods designed before the date an EPA restriction rule is published, so those parts could keep using chemicals the EPA has restricted for other uses.

The EPA could still regulate an exempted part, but only after finding in a risk evaluation, backed by substantial evidence, that the part alone contributes significantly to risk to the general population or to a vulnerable subpopulation.
Even where regulation is allowed, the bill requires a transition period of at least 10 years before any restriction on replacement parts takes effect.

The bill also bars the EPA from prohibiting the manufacture, processing, or import of a chemical to the extent it is needed to make the exempted parts, with procedures keeping that supply limited to replacement-part manufacturers.

analysis.who_pays: People exposed to chemicals through replacement parts — including the vulnerable subpopulations the EPA's own risk evaluations identify — would continue to be exposed for years longer, because the EPA would have to prove a part is risky all by itself, something individual parts rarely are. The EPA's ability to carry out chemical restrictions under the Toxic Substances Control Act would be narrowed, and restricted chemicals would keep entering homes and waste streams through repaired products.
analysis.who_pays_short: People exposed to restricted chemicals in parts

drawbacks.text: The bill would let chemicals that the EPA has risk-evaluated keep being used in replacement parts for every product designed before a rule is published, which can cover products made decades earlier, extending exposure for the general population and vulnerable groups.

The 'part alone' test sets a high bar: chemical risk often comes from combined exposures, so requiring proof that a single part significantly drives the risk would make regulation of parts difficult in practice.

The ban on prohibiting upstream manufacture or import of chemicals needed for exempted parts would undercut the EPA's authority to restrict a chemical's production overall, since a major channel of use would remain lawful.

The strongest good-faith objection to the bill's critics is that it is unnecessary as written: the EPA can already grant narrower exemptions where restriction would cut off needed parts, so a blanket exemption swaps a tailored tool for a broad carve-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine consumer concern on the bill's side: if a chemical restriction swept in replacement parts, owners of functioning older cars and appliances could lose the parts needed to keep them running. But the bill addresses that with a blanket, effectively permanent exemption rather than a case-by-case carve-out, and it hands the burden to the EPA to prove each part risky on its own — a showing that combined-exposure science rarely supports. The result is a large, durable rollback of chemical regulation for parts, with the public bearing the exposure cost and industry bearing little.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Richard Hudson introduced the bill on January 21, 2026, with Representative Troy Balderson as the one cosponsor, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The action history shows no further steps since the referral: no subcommittee or full committee consideration, no floor action, and no vote of any kind.

The bill would amend section 6 of the Toxic Substances Control Act to require the EPA to exempt replacement parts for pre-rule-designed complex products, and to limit EPA's ability to restrict those parts or the chemicals used to make them.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, current EPA chemical restrictions apply unchanged and manufacturers have not yet received the exemption they are seeking; the parties better off right now are those defending the existing rules. The bill's backers lose nothing by waiting, since a favorable Congress could still move it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Current chemical rules stand; no one has moved

against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has not scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill has seen no committee action since January 2026.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans are attached to the bill — one sponsor and one cosponsor — and no member has opposed it on the record, so no partisan split has actually formed yet.

industries.industry: Replacement parts and complex durable goods manufacturers (autos, appliances, electronics)
industries.note: The bill guarantees these manufacturers can keep making and selling parts with restricted chemicals for every product designed before a rule is published, sparing them reformulation costs. Their interest in avoiding chemical restrictions diverges from the public's interest in less exposure, though it lines up with owners of older products who want parts to stay available.

The bill bars the EPA from prohibiting manufacture, processing, or import of a chemical needed for exempted replacement parts, preserving a market for substances the EPA has restricted for other uses. That continued supply is what carries the exposure cost to the public.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, one cosponsor, and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill sits at the stage where most bills stall: it would need the Energy and Commerce Committee to hold a hearing and markup before any floor vote could happen. Unless the chair schedules action, it is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress.
